summary: For ages 10–11, construct a complete line graph from a table of continuous measurements and use it to answer questions. Choose labelled numerical scales, preserve actual time spacing, plot paired readings and join in order. Read observations, describe trends, compute differences and estimate between observations under an explicit straight-line assumption. With unequal intervals, distinguish total change from change per hour.
misconceptions: Treats rows as equally spaced times when the time gaps differ.
Uses a changing numerical scale along an axis.
Swaps coordinates or reads graph height without the time/value units.
Treats a line segment as an exact record of every unmeasured value.
Names the highest point when asked for the largest change or fastest increase.

activities.title: Build a line graph from a table
steps: Use temperatures at 09:00 12°C, 10:00 16°C, 11:00 18°C, 12:00 17°C and 13:00 19°C. Name time as the horizontal variable and temperature as the vertical variable.
Choose equal-hour spacing and a vertical scale covering 12–19°C; a 0–20°C axis with equal 2°C intervals and clear minor divisions is one option. Label time and temperature (°C).
Plot each pair yourself, check its horizontal and vertical coordinates, join points in time order, and add an informative title.
Compare your plotted points with the table before viewing a worked answer.
activities.insight: A line graph is a constructed mapping between paired measurements and labelled numerical axes, not a copied silhouette.

activities.title: Read, compare and estimate on your graph
steps: Identify the highest recorded temperature and the interval with the largest increase.
Find the 10:00–11:00 change, then estimate 10:30 using the straight segment and state the assumption.
Explain a flat or falling segment in terms of the measured quantity; distinguish the line from a picture of a journey or landscape.
activities.insight: Point height, change and estimated intermediate values answer different questions.

activities.title: Keep unequal time intervals honest
steps: Plot a second table: 09:00 10°C, 10:00 14°C and 12:00 20°C. Make the 10:00–12:00 gap twice the 09:00–10:00 gap.
Compare the first rise, 4°C in one hour, with the later rise, 6°C in two hours. Calculate change per hour before saying which interval warmed faster.
Explain why the larger total increase is not necessarily the steeper rise when time intervals differ.
activities.insight: Numerical time spacing determines the plotted rate: 4°C per hour is faster than 3°C per hour although 6°C is the larger total rise.

activities.title: Explain when a line is useful
steps: Compare a temperature table indexed by time with favourite-fruit counts by unordered category. Choose a line graph for the former and bars for the latter.
Explain what an intermediate time means, and why halfway between apple and banana has no corresponding ordered category value.
Check that your own graph could be read by someone who did not see the original table.
activities.insight: Graph choice depends on the variables and their ordering; connecting points does not manufacture meaningful intermediate data.

checkQuestion: Give the table 09:00 12°C, 10:00 16°C, 11:00 18°C, 12:00 17°C, 13:00 19°C. Ask the learner to construct a labelled line graph from blank axes, choose and explain a scale, identify the highest observed value and largest hourly rise, calculate the 10:00–11:00 change, and estimate 10:30 under a straight-line assumption. Then ask how the horizontal positions should change for readings at 09:00, 10:00 and 12:00.
checkAnswer: The pupil constructs a graph with time and temperature units, equal numerical scale intervals and all five correctly paired points joined in order. Highest: 13:00, 19°C. Largest hourly rise: 09:00–10:00, 4°C. The 10:00–11:00 change is +2°C and the straight-line 10:30 estimate is 17°C; the actual value is not known. For 09:00, 10:00, 12:00 the last horizontal gap is twice the first.
